1.note: The words **Hallelu Yah** are Hebrew words, containing a plural command to praise Yahweh. You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
**Yah** is a shortened form of the name “Yahweh,” the God of Israel. You could use the full name if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Yahweh]

The psalmist is speaking to his own soul, which cannot hear him. He is doing this to express how strongly he feels about praising Yahweh. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about himself. Alternate translation: [I will praise Yahweh with all of my being]

The psalmist is using one part of himself, his **soul**, to mean all of himself in the act of praising. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I myself will praise Yahweh]

2.q: אֲהַלְלָ֣ה יְהוָ֣ה בְּ⁠חַיָּ֑⁠י אֲזַמְּרָ֖ה לֵֽ⁠אלֹהַ֣⁠י בְּ⁠עוֹדִֽ⁠י
2.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Let me praise Yahweh my God with music for as long as I live]

3.note: The psalmist is using the phrase **the son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean a human being. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in any human being]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [ability to save]

4.note: The pronouns **His** and **he** refer to the mortal person described in the previous verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [That person’s breath goes out, that person returns to his ground]

The psalmist is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase **His breath goes out**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [He dies]

The psalmist is referring to the burial of a dead body in a polite way by using the phrase **he returns to his ground**. This alludes to the account in Genesis where God formed man from the ground. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [his body decays and becomes dust again]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **thoughts**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what he was planning comes to nothing]

5.note: The psalmist is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of joy. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. If not, you could say what the psalmist was feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh, how happy is]

The psalmist is not using the possessive form **the God of Jacob** to indicate that Jacob possesses or controls God. Rather the psalmist is using these words to indicate that God is the one whom Jacob worshiped. Alternate translation: [the one who has the God whom Jacob worshiped for his help]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **help** and **hope**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [to help him; he confidently waits for Yahweh his God]

6.note: The psalmist is referring to all of creation by naming its major components, **the heavens** and **the earth**, and then adding **the sea and all that is in them**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [everything that exists]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **faithfulness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [faithful to his promises]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [judging fairly]

The psalmist is using the adjective **oppressed** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for those whom others oppress]
The psalmist is using one kind of food, **bread**, to mean food in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [nourishment]

The psalmist is using the adjective **hungry** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to hungry people]

8.note: Here, **opening** represents giving sight to. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [giving sight to the blind]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is opening the eyes of the blind]

The psalmist is using the adjective **blind** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [blind people]

The psalmist is speaking of those who are discouraged or oppressed as if they were people who were physically **bowed down**. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is lifting up those who are discouraged]

The psalmist is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

9.note: The word **but** introduces a contrast between how Yahweh treats the vulnerable and how he treats the wicked. Yahweh protects the sojourners, the orphan, and the widow, **but** he overturns the way of the wicked. Use a natural way in your language to indicate this contrast. Alternate translation: [however, the way of the wicked, he overturns]

The psalmist is speaking of how a person lives and behaves as if it were a **way** or path that the person walks on. If this image does not communicate well in your language, you could express this as a comparison or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but the plans of the wicked]

The psalmist is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wicked]

10.note: The psalmist is leaving out the verb that would naturally appear in this phrase. The reader can supply it from the first part of the verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could supply this verb explicitly. Alternate translation: [your God, Zion, reigns to generation and generation]

The psalmist is speaking to the city of Zion, which cannot hear him. He is doing this to express how strongly he feels about Yahweh’s eternal reign. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate these words as if he were speaking directly to the people about Zion. Alternate translation: [the God of Zion]

The psalmist is using the phrase **to generation and generation** as a common expression of the culture to mean “forever”. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for all time]

You will need to decide if you will use these words in their Hebrew form or if you will instead translate the meaning into your language. Either approach has broad support. If you use the Hebrew words, you could spell them the way that they sound in your language and then put the translation in a footnote. Alternate translation: [Halleluia] or [Praise Yah]
